extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, applicants, examiners, and students interested in European Patent Convention inventive step law
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment of inventive step for European patent applications under Article 56 EPC, primarily using the EPO 'problem-and-solution' approach and related case-law guidance. Covers selection of closest prior art, formulation of the objective technical problem, obviousness (could/would), and special cases (partial problems, mixed technical/non-technical features, problem inventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step (Article 56 EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention, having regard to the state of the art, must not be obvious to a person skilled in the art (Article 56 EPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central legal provision; the EPO Boards of Appeal have developed the problem-and-solution approach to assess whether an invention involves an inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-and-solution approach (three-step method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess inventive step by (1) identifying the closest prior art and differences between the invention and that art; (2) determining the technical effect(s) of the differences and defining the objective technical problem; and (3) examining whether the claimed solution to that problem is obvious to the skilled person in view of the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used predominantly by EPO Examining Divisions, Opposition Divisions and Boards of Appeal as an objective way of deciding inventive step (see T 24/81 and subsequent case law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closest prior art / appropriate starting point
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the most promising starting point (closest prior art) from which a skilled person could have arrived at the claimed invention; the closest prior art is the 'most promising springboard to the invention' and need not be unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The expression 'appropriate starting point' recognises that inventive assessment may be started from more than one piece of prior art; the assessment may need to be repeated from different starting points. The closest prior art can be a document or a public prior use. The notional skilled person is assumed to be aware of the totality of prior art pertinent to the relevant area (Article 54(2) EPC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining distinguishing features and technical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the feature(s) distinguishing the claimed subject‑matter from the closest prior art and determine the technical effect(s) produced by those distinguishing features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The objective technical problem (task) is then framed as how to adapt or modify the closest prior art to obtain the identified technical effect(s). Any alleged technical effect must be proved or at least be 'plausibly solved' at the filing date to rely on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulation of the objective technical problem — no pointer to the solution
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective technical problem must be formulated without including a part of the solution provided by the invention (i.e., without pointers to the solution), to avoid ex post facto hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The problem used need not be identical to that in the application and may be reformulated if necessary. If an alleged effect is not proved, the problem must be reformulated. Providing experimental data is not always required if the technical problem was at least plausibly solved at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Could–would approach for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing obviousness, ask whether the prior art, as a whole, would (not merely could) have prompted the skilled person, faced with the objectively formulated technical problem, to modify or adapt the closest prior art so as to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The focus is on whether the prior art would have incited the skilled person to act because of an expectation of solving the problem or obtaining some improvement — not merely whether it was possible. This distinguishes theoretical combinations ('could') from realistic, motivated combinations ('would').

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason/motivation for combining prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a reason for combining two or more pieces of prior art, and that reason must have existed for the skilled person before the filing or priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent a pre-existing motivation or teaching providing a reason to combine, a later-assembled combination may be considered an ex post facto reconstruction and not indicative of lack of inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial problems (multiple independent partial problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where different distinguishing feature-sets solve different independent partial problems (i.e., no single technical effect achieved by all distinguishing features taken in combination), each set is assessed independently as a partial problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each partial problem and its corresponding distinguishing features separately for the purposes of assessing inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comvik approach for mixed technical and non-technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions mixing technical and non-technical features, non-technical features (those in fields excluded under Article 52(2) and (3) EPC) are normally ignored for inventive step assessment unless they interact with the technical subject‑matter to solve a technical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A positive assessment of inventive step can only be based on elements/aspects for which a technical effect can be established. Technically non-functional modifications are irrelevant to inventive step even if the skilled person would not think of such modifications. Assessing whether a feature contributes to technical character can be difficult in practice (T 641/00 and follow-up decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical effect must be credibly obtained across claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: An alleged technical effect relied upon to define the objective technical problem must be credibly obtained throughout the whole range covered by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the effect is not credibly achieved across the claimed scope, it cannot be taken into account when defining the objective technical problem or when assessing inventive step (see case law references such as T 1214/09, T 0960/15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence requirement for alleged advantages or technical effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleged advantages or technical effects referred to by the applicant/proprietor must be supported by sufficient evidence; mere assertion without support cannot be relied upon in determining the underlying problem and assessing inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence is lacking, the problem must be reformulated. Providing experimental data in the application is not strictly required if the technical problem is at least plausibly solved at filing, but unsupported claims of advantage are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem inventions (discovery of an unrecognised problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of an unrecognised problem may, in certain circumstances, lead to patentable subject‑matter even if the claimed solution is retrospectively trivial or obvious; if the identification of the problem is not obvious, the solution to it cannot be obvious either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking a 'problem invention', negative assessments of inventive step should explain how the skilled person would have become aware of the problem without that being inventive in itself. See T 2/83 and related case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public prior use and non-documentary prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The closest prior art may be a public prior use (not only a document); features made available by public prior use can be considered the closest state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that public prior uses are treated consistently with documentary prior art under Article 54(2) EPC when selecting the starting point for the problem-and-solution approach.
